Period schedule:

Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem — Read-Aloud and First Thinking

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p.36): why focus matters and listing rhyming words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud from Textbook pp.35–36 with clear expression, pausing at each stanza. Students follow in their books and listen for the repeating lines about work and play.

Choral reading: students and teacher read the poem together twice, voice rising on the refrain “Work while you work, / Play while you play.” Teacher points to end-rhyme pairs on the board (play/way, might/right, well/tell, away/play) and asks students to clap each time a rhyming pair lands.

Let us Think — A. (“why focus matters and listing rhyme pairs”): teacher poses questions 1 and 2 orally; students share answers aloud, then write short responses in their notebooks. Teacher draws out the poet’s warning against half-hearted effort.

Brief whole-class share: two or three students read their answers to question 2 (rhyming words). Teacher confirms the four rhyme pairs on the board and invites students to notice the poem’s orderly four-line pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s simple ABCB rhyme scheme and didactic tone make it easy to read aloud confidently — model steady, unhurried pacing to echo the poem’s own message of doing one thing well. Students often find ‘trifled’ unfamiliar; a quick gesture-based explanation (‘wasted carelessly’) before the second read prevents confusion. Questions 3 and 4 from Let us Think are left unanchored here and may be used as an informal self-study prompt by students who finish early.

periods.activity_title: Speaking About What We Do — Free Time and Picture Talk

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think (p.36): discuss what you like doing in free time.
Let us Speak (p.37): describe the Madhubani painting and frame present-continuous sentences.

time_bands.activity: Having chanted the poem together, teacher reopens the idea of work and play: students pair up and take turns answering “What do you like doing in your free time?” Each partner listens, then reports one thing their partner said to the class.

Let us Speak (p.37): teacher directs students to the Madhubani painting in the textbook and leads a picture walk, eliciting observations stanza by stanza — “What is this person doing? And that group?” Students call out actions; teacher notes vivid verbs on the board.

Teacher models the sentence frame “Who | Is/Are | Doing What” from the textbook table on the board, then guides students to make five sentences orally in pairs before writing at least seven in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, prompting use of ‘is’ vs ‘are’ correctly.
Quick share-out: four students read one sentence each. Class listens and gives a thumbs-up if the subject-verb agreement sounds right. Teacher corrects gently on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The Madhubani painting shows many simultaneous actions, which naturally sparks the poem’s contrast between focused single-tasking and chaotic multi-tasking — a light connection worth naming if students notice it. Watch for subject-verb agreement errors with plural subjects (‘two girls are’ not ‘two girls is’); this is the most common slip at this level.

periods.activity_title: Words and the Silent ‘l’ — Meaning Match and Listening Drill

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.36): match might, useful, moments with meanings.
Let us Listen (p.39): circle words where the ‘l’ is silent.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn — A. (“match poem words with meanings”): teacher writes ‘might’, ‘useful’, and ‘moments’ on the board and asks students to recall where each word appears in the poem. Students then complete the matching task in their textbooks independently before a whole-class check.

Teacher leads a short contextual-prediction round: “If you do something with all your might, what does that feel like?” Students suggest synonyms (strength, force, effort) and teacher writes them alongside ‘might’ on the board, reinforcing meaning through context.

Let us Listen — (“silent-‘l’ circle drill”): teacher reads each word from Textbook p.39 aloud clearly, once, then pauses. Students listen and circle words where they do not hear the ‘l’ sound. After all 15 words, teacher reads the list once more for self-correction.

Whole-class debrief: teacher writes the full word list on the board and cold-calls students to say “I hear the ‘l’” or “The ‘l’ is silent” for each. Correct answers are circled together; teacher writes the six silent-‘l’ words (calm, palm, calf, chalk, talk, balm) in a coloured box and invites students to repeat them in chorus.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse ‘might’ (strength) with the modal verb ‘might’ (possibility) — a quick sentence pair on the board (‘She might come’ vs ‘Do it with all your might’) resolves this efficiently. For the silent-‘l’ drill, pronounce each word at natural speaking pace rather than over-articulating, so students hear authentic speech patterns rather than artificially exaggerated ones.

periods.activity_title: My Daily Routine — Table, Paragraph and Peer Sharing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (pp.38–40): fill daily-routine table and classify activities as work or play.
Let us Write (pp.38–40): write the routine as a three-part paragraph using the sentence frames.

time_bands.activity: Teacher thinks aloud and fills a sample routine table on the board — three activities, each ticked as work or play — modelling how to choose specific times and honest labels. Students open Textbook pp.38–40 and begin filling their own six-row table, guided by the teacher’s model.

Students complete the table independently. Teacher circulates, prompting: “Is cooking breakfast work or play for you? Why?” When students finish, teacher quickly shows how the table’s rows become the material for a paragraph.

Let us Write — paragraph frames (“My Routine / At School / At Home paragraph frames”): teacher reads the first frame aloud from the textbook, filling in sample blanks on the board while thinking aloud. Students then write all three frames in their notebooks using their own table entries as the source. Teacher supports students who struggle with the ‘At Home’ open lines.

Unhurried paired share: each student reads one sentence from their paragraph to a partner. Partners listen and give one specific compliment (“I liked how you said …”). Teacher takes two or three volunteers to share with the whole class and praises vivid time-detail.

periods.teacher_notes: The two writing tasks are designed to flow into each other — the table is the raw material for the paragraph — so both are anchored in this unit and completed together. Watch for students who classify every activity as ‘work’; invite them to re-read the poem’s second stanza to prompt a richer distinction between wholehearted effort and joyful recreation.

periods.activity_title: Riddles and Holiday Drawings — Guessing, Reasoning and Creating

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.41): guess the three riddles through reasoning and discussion.
Let us Do — B. (p.41): draw or paste pictures of favourite holiday activities.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces riddles as a playful puzzle tradition and sets the ground rule: no calling out the answer — whisper it to the teacher or write it on a slip. This keeps everyone thinking rather than listening for the first answer.

Let us Do — A. (“guess the three riddles”): teacher reads each riddle from Textbook p.41 aloud twice, then gives students thinking time. For Riddle 1, teacher prompts: “Thirty white horses — what in your body comes in sets and is on a ‘red hill’?” After students guess, teacher reveals and discusses the imagery. Riddles 2 and 3 follow in the same pattern.

Let us Do — B. (“draw or paste holiday activities”): students use the space in their textbook or a fresh page to draw at least two activities they enjoy in holidays. Teacher encourages labelling each drawing with an action phrase, connecting back to the present-continuous sentences practised when exploring the Madhubani painting.

Gallery moment: students hold up or pass around their drawings. Teacher invites three students to describe one of their pictures in a sentence (“I am flying a kite on the beach”). Class listens and gives a quick clap of appreciation.

periods.teacher_notes: Riddle 1 (teeth) and Riddle 2 (a candle) rely on imagery students may not immediately decode; prompting them to visualise the description physically (‘chomp’, ‘shorter she grows’) is more productive than giving hints about the answer category. Riddle 3 (a coconut) is the most accessible and can anchor students who find the first two challenging.
materials: Old newspapers or magazines (optional, for cutting and pasting)

periods.activity_title: Revisiting the Poem — Recitation, Rhyme and Reflection

time_bands.activity: Repeated reading of the whole poem: students open Textbook pp.35–36 and read the poem aloud in unison twice. On the third reading, one half of the class reads the ‘work’ lines and the other half reads the ‘play’ lines, reinforcing the poem’s central contrast.

Recitation without the book: teacher invites volunteers to recite one stanza each from memory. After each stanza, class responds with the refrain (“Work while you work, / And play while you play”) together, making recitation a shared celebration rather than a test.

Quick word game revisiting the silent-‘l’ words and poem vocabulary: teacher says a word (‘chalk’, ‘might’, ‘balm’, ‘useful’, ‘moments’) and students signal thumbs-up if they hear the ‘l’ or show a hand gesture for its meaning. Pairs then challenge each other with one word each.

Formative writing check: students write two sentences of their own inspired by the poem’s advice — one about how they work and one about how they play — without using the poem’s exact words. Teacher circulates, giving brief verbal feedback on word choice and the work/play distinction.

Closing whole-class share: teacher asks “What is the one line from this poem you will remember?” Students call out their chosen line; teacher writes four or five favourites on the board as a parting display. Class reads them in chorus once before closing their books.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit draws on the poem’s language, the rhyme pairs students identified, the silent-‘l’ words, and the work/play distinction from the writing routine — revisiting what the chapter built rather than introducing new content. The formative writing check is deliberately brief so that every student, including slower writers, can finish within the available time.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 35 beginning “Things done by halves.” What does the poet mean by ‘done by halves’?

options.label: A
options.text: Tasks that are shared equally between two people.

options.label: B
options.text: Tasks that are started but not finished properly.

options.label: C
options.text: Tasks that are too difficult for one person alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Tasks that take exactly half the usual time.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be reading ‘halves’ as division of labour rather than incompleteness.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is interpreting ‘halves’ as a time measure rather than an effort measure.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student is confusing difficulty level with the poem’s message about incomplete effort.

items.source_context: Focus, effort, work-play balance; end-rhyme pairs play/way, might/right, well/tell, away/play.
items.item_stem: The poem ends by repeating its opening lines: “Work while you work, / And play while you play.” Why do you think the poet chose to end the poem with the same words it began with? Write 1–2 sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The poet repeats the opening lines at the end to make the message feel like a rule worth remembering, like a refrain that stays in the reader’s mind. The repetition reinforces the idea that focusing fully on whatever you are doing — work or play — is the most important habit.

items.item_stem: Look at the Madhubani painting on Textbook page 37. Choose any two people you can see in the painting and say one sentence about each, using the words ‘is’ or ‘are’.

options.text: In the painting, each person is doing more than three activities at the same time.
The sentence ‘Two girls are going to school’ follows the Who – Is/Are – Doing What pattern.
When we talk about one person doing something right now, we use ‘are’.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is false: each person in the painting is engaged in one activity, not three or more simultaneously. Statement 2 is true: the sentence ‘Two girls are going to school’ correctly follows the Who – Is/Are – Doing What frame. Statement 3 is false: when talking about one person, we use ‘is’, not ‘are’.

items.item_stem:
Complete the sentence below to make a correct sentence about a morning activity:

Every morning at 7 a.m., I _______________ and then _______________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any grammatically correct pair of morning activities, for example: “Every morning at 7 a.m., I brush my teeth and then eat breakfast.” The two blanks should be filled with action verbs describing real routine activities.
